levels.beginner: An access control entry is one line on a guest list: it names a person or group and says what they may or may not do with something.
levels.maker: Each entry either grants or denies permissions to a user or group. SharePoint builds on the Windows security model, so you meet these entries when permissions are inherited or checked. Entries are collected into an [[access-control-list]].
levels.architect: An entry sits in an object's discretionary list (DACL), where it grants or denies access, or in its system list (SACL), where it says which security events to audit or sets the Windows Integrity Level. The order and type of entries decide the final access result.

terms.summary: An access control entry is one line on a guest list: it names a person or group and says what they may or may not do with something.

levels.beginner: An access control list is the full guest list for a door: every person or group and what each is allowed to do.
levels.maker: It is the set of [[access-control-entry|access control entries]] for a whole object, a group of its properties, or a single property. It defines the access given to each security principal, such as a user or a group.
levels.architect: In Windows-based systems the list can be attached at several levels of granularity. Whenever a principal asks for access, the system walks the entries to decide the result, so the list is the unit that security checks are evaluated against.

terms.summary: An access control list is the full guest list for a door: every person or group and what each is allowed to do.

levels.beginner: An access URL is the address the search robot uses to reach a file or page when it collects information for search.
levels.maker: When search crawls content it needs an internal address for each item. That is the access URL, and it is not always the address people see in the search results. Keep the two apart when you troubleshoot why an item is missing.
levels.architect: The access URL is the internal URL a crawler uses to identify and fetch an item. It can differ from the display URL shown to users, and the crawl log records results against the display URL. See [[crawl-log]].

terms.summary: An access URL is the address the search robot uses to reach a file or page when it collects information for search.

levels.beginner: An action is something an agent can do for you rather than just say, such as sending an email or updating a record.
levels.maker: [[agent|Agents]] use actions, also called tools, to automate steps and connect to other systems. Actions can be provided by services such as MCP servers or REST APIs, and in Copilot Studio they can also be [[connector|connectors]] or flows.
levels.architect: Tool calling invokes configured MCP or API actions. You define the inputs and outputs, the authentication and any confirmations, and make the service behave reliably. Ask for confirmation before an action changes data, and give the identity that the action uses only the access it needs.

terms.summary: An action is something an agent can do for you rather than just say, such as sending an email or updating a record.

levels.beginner: An activity feed is like a news ticker of what the people, documents and topics you follow have been up to.
levels.maker: It collects notifications and updates about people, documents and tags that you follow, so you can catch up in one place instead of visiting each item. It is one of the social features of SharePoint.
levels.architect: The feed is built from user-profile and social data, so what appears depends on what a person follows. Treat it as a presentation of changes rather than as an audit log, because it only reflects the things followed.

terms.summary: An activity feed is like a news ticker of what the people, documents and topics you follow have been up to.

levels.beginner: An activity flow is a recipe being followed right now, one step after another.
levels.maker: It is a running instance of a workflow made of a sequence of action instances and activity model instances. You can put the steps in any order, but together they form one activity flow.
levels.architect: The flow is the runtime counterpart of its definition: action instances and [[activity-model]] instances are sequenced to make a single flow. Distinguish the running flow from the template that defines it.

terms.summary: An activity flow is a recipe being followed right now, one step after another.

levels.beginner: An activity model is a ready-made routine, like a saved checklist of steps that you can reuse.
levels.maker: It is a predefined sequence of actions. Instead of rebuilding the same steps each time, you reuse the model inside a bigger [[activity-flow]].
levels.architect: Models are building blocks: an [[activity-flow]] can mix single actions and activity model instances in any order. Reuse them to keep workflows consistent and to avoid copying the same sequence into several places.

terms.summary: An activity model is a ready-made routine, like a saved checklist of steps that you can reuse.

levels.beginner: An Adaptive Card is a small, tidy panel with text, pictures and buttons that appears inside a chat, like a mini form.
levels.maker: Cards let an [[agent]] or a workflow show information and ask for a choice in a consistent layout, wherever the conversation happens. You describe the card once and each app draws it in its own style.
levels.architect: A card is described in JSON, and the host application renders it to match its own look. Keep cards small and avoid putting secrets in them, because their content is visible in the conversation.

terms.summary: An Adaptive Card is a small, tidy panel with text, pictures and buttons that appears inside a chat, like a mini form.

levels.beginner: An after event is like a thank-you note sent once a job has finished.
levels.maker: SharePoint raises events when something happens, such as an item being added. An after event runs its handler only once the action has already completed, and it does not hold things up.
levels.architect: After events are asynchronous: the handler runs after the action that raised the event is complete, so it cannot stop or change that action. Use [[before-event|before events]] when you need to block or alter an operation.

terms.summary: An after event is like a thank-you note sent once a job has finished.

levels.beginner: An agent is an AI assistant that can do a job for you, such as answering questions about a policy or booking a room. You tell it what it should do, what it may know and what it may act on.
levels.maker: An agent follows instructions, draws on [[knowledge-source|knowledge sources]] and uses [[agent-action|actions]] to get things done. You can build one in [[copilot-studio]] or [[agent-builder]], or, for Microsoft 365 Copilot, as a [[declarative-agent]] or a [[custom-engine-agent]].
levels.architect: An agent has an [[orchestrator]] that plans and calls tools, a [[large-language-model]] for reasoning and language, knowledge and actions, and a user experience layer in a place such as Teams. Treat retrieved content and tool responses as untrusted input, and enforce authorisation in the services the agent calls.

terms.summary: An agent is an AI assistant that can do a job for you, such as answering questions about a policy or booking a room. You tell it what it should do, what it may know and what it may act on.

levels.beginner: Agent 365 is a control panel for the AI agents an organisation uses, so someone can see them and keep them in check.
levels.maker: It is described as a management and governance layer for discovering, securing, controlling and observing agents across an organisation. It matters once many people start creating [[agent|agents]] and the organisation needs an overview.
levels.architect: Treat it as the governance side of agents: inventory, access, security and monitoring. It sits alongside the wider [[copilot-control-system]], and its detailed capabilities can change, so confirm current behaviour in Microsoft's own documentation.

terms.summary: Agent 365 is a control panel for the AI agents an organisation uses, so someone can see them and keep them in check.

levels.beginner: Agent Builder is a quick way for people to create a simple agent for themselves or their team, mostly by describing what it should do.
levels.maker: It is aimed at everyday users rather than specialists. It was renamed Copilot Studio Lite in September 2025 and went back to Agent Builder in November 2025, so you will see both names. For more control, such as connecting other systems and managing agents at scale, use [[copilot-studio]].
levels.architect: Treat agents made this way as lightweight and give each one a clear owner. Decide who may create and share them, what knowledge they may use, and when a fuller build in [[copilot-studio]] is justified. Check current capabilities, because the product has changed name and scope more than once.

terms.summary: Agent Builder is a quick way for people to create a simple agent for themselves or their team, mostly by describing what it should do.

levels.beginner: Agentic AI is AI that can work through several steps to reach a goal, instead of just answering one question.
levels.maker: Where plain [[generative-ai]] produces a single reply to a single request, agentic systems plan, use tools and carry on until a task is done. An [[agent]] is the usual way you meet it.
levels.architect: The pattern combines a model, instructions, memory, [[tool-calling|tools]] and a loop that decides the next step. Because it can act, it needs tighter permissions, logging and [[human-in-the-loop|human review]] than a chat reply does.

terms.summary: Agentic AI is AI that can work through several steps to reach a goal, instead of just answering one question.

levels.beginner: AI Builder lets you add ready-made AI skills, such as reading text from a form, to apps and flows without needing data science knowledge.
levels.maker: You pick a model type, such as extracting information from documents or classifying text, and use it inside [[power-apps]] or [[power-automate]]. Check which models are currently available in your region before you plan around them.
levels.architect: AI Builder models run as a service in an [[environment]] and use capacity, so plan capacity and measure accuracy on your own documents. Related document-focused features also exist elsewhere in Microsoft 365; see [[document-processing]].

terms.summary: AI Builder lets you add ready-made AI skills, such as reading text from a form, to apps and flows without needing data science knowledge.

levels.beginner: An AI model is the trained "brain" inside an AI tool: it has learned patterns from lots of examples and uses them to produce an answer.
levels.maker: Different models are good at different things, such as writing, images or numbers. Products like [[microsoft-365-copilot]] wrap a model with extra services for search, security and the apps you use.
levels.architect: A model transforms an input into a predicted or generated output. In Copilot the model is only one part: [[orchestration]], [[grounding]], permissions and safety controls surround it, so the same model can behave differently in different products.

terms.summary: An AI model is the trained "brain" inside an AI tool: it has learned patterns from lots of examples and uses them to produce an answer.

levels.beginner: AI safety is the set of habits and controls that stop an AI from causing harm or doing something unexpected.
levels.maker: It covers harmful or misleading output, security attacks and unintended actions. Admins and builders use content filters, [[guardrail|guardrails]], testing and review to reduce those risks.
levels.architect: Safety work spans design, testing and operation: for example [[red-teaming]], [[moderation]], [[prompt-injection]] defences and monitoring in production. It overlaps with [[responsible-ai]], which is the broader set of principles.

terms.summary: AI safety is the set of habits and controls that stop an AI from causing harm or doing something unexpected.

levels.beginner: AI-generated content is anything an AI wrote or made for you: text, images, summaries, code and so on.
levels.maker: Treat it as a starting point. It is made from your instructions and whatever context the tool could see, so it can be wrong or miss the point, and you remain responsible for what you send or publish.
levels.architect: Because output is produced probabilistically, apply [[verification]] and sensitivity-label rules to it as you would to any other content. Some organisations also track or mark AI-generated material for compliance.

terms.summary: AI-generated content is anything an AI wrote or made for you: text, images, summaries, code and so on.

levels.beginner: An alert subscription is a request that says: tell me by message whenever this thing changes.
levels.maker: You ask to be told when something you care about changes, such as a document, web page, list item, site or other resource. The messages are sent for you automatically once your chosen conditions are met.
levels.architect: A subscription is a request to receive an Internet message when user-defined criteria are met. The messages are generated automatically when matching items change, so the criteria you define are what keep the volume manageable.

terms.summary: An alert subscription is a request that says: tell me by message whenever this thing changes.

levels.beginner: An alternate account is a second login for the same person, kept in a different place from their main one.
levels.maker: It is an extra user account that lives in a different domain but within the same forest as the person's primary account. You see the idea when one person needs separate sign-ins for different kinds of work.
levels.architect: The extra account is in a different domain, but still within the same forest as the primary account. Treat it as a separate security principal when you assign permissions.

terms.summary: An alternate account is a second login for the same person, kept in a different place from their main one.

levels.beginner: Analyst is a ready-made Copilot helper that is good at working with numbers and data.
levels.maker: It is a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent aimed at data analysis, calculations and structured reasoning, turning business information into insights. Pair it with [[researcher]], which is aimed at wide research across sources.
levels.architect: Like other built-in agents, what it can read depends on the signed-in user's permissions and on how the organisation has enabled it. Availability and licensing can change, so check current documentation.

terms.summary: Analyst is a ready-made Copilot helper that is good at working with numbers and data.

levels.beginner: The app catalog is a special SharePoint site where an organisation keeps the custom apps and extensions it has approved for its sites.
levels.maker: There is one tenant-level app catalog, and individual site collections can have their own. Developers' [[spfx]] packages are uploaded to the catalog. An admin can make a solution available to all sites at once, or site owners can add it to their own sites.
levels.architect: The tenant app catalog is created by an administrator. A site collection app catalog is added with PowerShell or the CLI for Microsoft 365 and scopes apps to that collection. SPFx packages (.sppkg) are stored in it and can be deployed tenant-wide. Older [[sharepoint-add-in|SharePoint Add-ins]] were also distributed through it.

terms.summary: The app catalog is a special SharePoint site where an organisation keeps the custom apps and extensions it has approved for its sites.

levels.beginner: App context is what Copilot can see about the thing you have open, such as the current document or email.
levels.maker: When you use Copilot inside an app, it can use the open file, message, workbook, presentation or meeting as background, so you don't have to paste it in.
levels.architect: It is one source of [[context]] added to the [[prompt]] before the model runs. It is similar to [[implicit-context]], which describes the same idea of the application supplying information automatically.

terms.summary: App context is what Copilot can see about the thing you have open, such as the current document or email.

levels.beginner: An app custom action is an extra button added to a site by an add-in, and it leads to more of that add-in's features.
levels.maker: It is a kind of [[custom-action]] that a [[sharepoint-add-in]] adds to a host site, linking people to the extra functionality inside the add-in. Because Add-ins have retired in SharePoint Online, the same job is done today with the [[spfx]].
levels.architect: The action is added to the [[host-web]] by the add-in and points at functionality in the add-in. Add-ins stopped working in SharePoint Online on 2 April 2026 but still exist on SharePoint Server, so expect to meet this term only in older or on-premises solutions.

terms.summary: An app custom action is an extra button added to a site by an add-in, and it leads to more of that add-in's features.

levels.beginner: An app part is a window on a page that shows a small piece of an add-in.
levels.maker: It is a component of a [[sharepoint-add-in]] that you place on a site page to expose what the add-in does. It plays a similar role to a [[web-part]], and today the [[spfx]] web part replaces it.
levels.architect: The app part is embedded in a page on the [[host-web]] and displays the add-in's content from the add-in itself. SharePoint Add-ins were retired in SharePoint Online on 2 April 2026, so it remains relevant for SharePoint Server only.

terms.summary: An app part is a window on a page that shows a small piece of an add-in.

levels.beginner: An app web is a small, separate SharePoint site created for a SharePoint-hosted add-in. It keeps the add-in's own files and lists apart from the site the add-in was installed on.
levels.maker: Each SharePoint-hosted [[sharepoint-add-in]] gets an app web on its own web address. It holds the add-in's pages, scripts and data, and it is removed when the add-in is uninstalled. The site where the add-in is installed is the [[host-web]].
levels.architect: The app web lives on an isolated app domain, which is why browser security stops its scripts from calling the [[host-web]] directly. Cross-domain requests are used instead. Because the app web is a separate site, it has its own permissions, and add-in permissions are granted to the add-in rather than to its users.

terms.summary: An app web is a small, separate SharePoint site created for a SharePoint-hosted add-in. It keeps the add-in's own files and lists apart from the site the add-in was installed on.

levels.beginner: The application directory is a folder on a search server where its working files for search are kept.
levels.maker: It is the directory on an index server or a query server that stores the files used to build, or to query, the full-text index catalog. Administrators care about it when they plan disk space for search.
levels.architect: The directory holds all the files for creating a full-text index catalog or for running queries against one. It exists on both index servers and query servers.

terms.summary: The application directory is a folder on a search server where its working files for search are kept.

levels.beginner: An application session is the time an application is open: it starts when you open it and ends when you close it.
levels.maker: The session starts when an application starts and ends when the application quits. Anything tied to the session, such as temporary state, lasts only for that period.
levels.architect: Use the session as the lifetime boundary for state that should not outlive one run of the application. When the application quits the session ends, so do not rely on it for storage across runs.

terms.summary: An application session is the time an application is open: it starts when you open it and ends when you close it.

levels.beginner: An audience identifier is the unique name tag that tells SharePoint which audience you mean.
levels.maker: Audiences group people so you can target content. Each audience has an identifier, which is a GUID or string, so it can be referred to without confusion even if two audiences have similar display names.
levels.architect: Use the identifier, not the display name, when you refer to an audience from code or configuration. It is a GUID or string that uniquely identifies the audience.

terms.summary: An audience identifier is the unique name tag that tells SharePoint which audience you mean.

levels.beginner: An audience rule is the entry test for a club: if you meet the conditions, you are in.
levels.maker: It is a set of logical conditions that decide whether a user profile can be a member of an audience. People who match the conditions are included automatically.
levels.architect: Rules evaluate user-profile information, so the quality of the [[user-profile-store]] data decides who matches. A rule is attached to an audience that is referred to by its [[audience-identifier]].

terms.summary: An audience rule is the entry test for a club: if you meet the conditions, you are in.

levels.beginner: Authentication is proving who you are, like showing your pass at the entrance.
levels.maker: Before Copilot or an agent uses any Microsoft 365 data it needs to know who is asking. Authentication answers "who are you?", while [[authorisation]] answers "what may you do?".
levels.architect: In Microsoft 365 identity is handled by [[microsoft-entra-id]]. Agents and connectors authenticate with user, app or managed identities, and [[single-sign-on]] lets one sign-in cover many apps.

terms.summary: Authentication is proving who you are, like showing your pass at the entrance.

levels.beginner: Authorisation decides what a person, Copilot or an agent is allowed to do once it is known who they are.
levels.maker: It covers reading, creating, changing and running things. Copilot only works with content that the user is already allowed to see, so authorisation limits what it can retrieve.
levels.architect: Rules come from permissions, [[role-based-access-control]] and policies. [[permission-trimming]] applies them at retrieval time, and [[least-privilege]] is the principle that keeps them narrow.

terms.summary: Authorisation decides what a person, Copilot or an agent is allowed to do once it is known who they are.

levels.beginner: An authoritative page is a web page an administrator has marked as especially trustworthy, so search shows it nearer the top.
levels.maker: A site collection administrator picks pages that are more relevant than others, typically the home page of the organisation's intranet. The higher the page's authority, the higher it tends to appear in search results.
levels.architect: Authority is expressed as an [[authority-level]], and the page is identified by its URL. Both names, authoritative page and authority page, refer to the same concept.

terms.summary: An authoritative page is a web page an administrator has marked as especially trustworthy, so search shows it nearer the top.

levels.beginner: The authority level is a score that says how important a page is: 0 is the best.
levels.maker: It is a floating-point number that marks a page as more relevant than others. The allowed values are 0, 1 or 2, and zero marks the most valuable [[authoritative-page]].
levels.architect: The value is a floating-point number restricted to 0, 1 and 2. Lower is more authoritative, so 0 is the highest level and the page then ranks higher in search results.

terms.summary: The authority level is a score that says how important a page is: 0 is the best.

levels.beginner: Autohost means the system puts the pieces of an add-in in the right places for you.
levels.maker: It is a way of deploying an add-in so that its components are placed on the proper hosts automatically and the add-in is isolated from other things. It saves developers from setting that up by hand for [[sharepoint-add-in|SharePoint Add-ins]].
levels.architect: With autohosting, deployment of the add-in components to the appropriate hosts and the isolation of the add-in are established automatically. As with other Add-in features it is retired in SharePoint Online and only a historical concern outside SharePoint Server.

terms.summary: Autohost means the system puts the pieces of an add-in in the right places for you.

levels.beginner: Autopilot is an AI helper that lives in your organisation and keeps working on its own between your requests, like a colleague with a standing job.
levels.maker: You give it a name, a role and a goal. It is hosted in the cloud, belongs to your tenant, has its own identity, memory and [[workspace]], and carries on working without waiting for each prompt. It is in private preview and is billed with usage-based [[copilot-credits]].
levels.architect: Because it has its own identity and acts over time, treat it like any other principal: give it [[least-privilege]] access, review what it does and set an owner. It was previously called Microsoft Scout; the name changed in September 2026, so older material may use the earlier name. Autopilots is also the name of Stage 5 in some Copilot adoption playbooks.

terms.summary: Autopilot is an AI helper that lives in your organisation and keeps working on its own between your requests, like a colleague with a standing job.

levels.beginner: An available site template is a layout you are allowed to pick when you create a new site.
levels.maker: It is a collection of predefined or user-defined settings, stored as a site definition configuration or a site template, that you can use when you create a site. Administrators can control which ones show up as choices.
levels.architect: The template can come from a [[site-definition-configuration]] or from a saved [[site-template]]. It is the XML-based collection of settings used to create the new site.

terms.summary: An available site template is a layout you are allowed to pick when you create a new site.

levels.beginner: Azure AI Foundry is Microsoft's workshop in the cloud for building, testing and running AI applications and agents.
levels.maker: Developers use it to choose models, connect data and tools, evaluate results and run what they build with enterprise controls. It is more developer-focused than low-code tools such as [[copilot-studio]].
levels.architect: It brings together models, tooling, [[evaluation]] and operations on Azure. Microsoft renames and reorganises its AI services fairly often, so check the current product name and features before planning.

terms.summary: Azure AI Foundry is Microsoft's workshop in the cloud for building, testing and running AI applications and agents.

levels.beginner: A background task is work an agent keeps doing while you get on with something else.
levels.maker: You start the job and don't have to stay in the conversation. When it finishes, or needs you, you can get a [[notification]].
levels.architect: Long-running work should be resumable and observable, with [[trace|traces]] or [[log|logs]], and with limits on what the agent can do while nobody is watching.

terms.summary: A background task is work an agent keeps doing while you get on with something else.

levels.beginner: Backward signing describes how a handwritten signature runs: from left to right, or the other way round.
levels.maker: It is a property of a handwritten signature stored as an image or an .ink file. It records the direction of the characters in the signature, either right-to-left or left-to-right.
levels.architect: The flag only describes direction of the characters in a stored signature, in an image or .ink file. Code that renders or compares signatures must read it to draw them correctly.

terms.summary: Backward signing describes how a handwritten signature runs: from left to right, or the other way round.

levels.beginner: The base view identifier is the number that picks out one saved way of looking at a list.
levels.maker: A list can have several views. This integer uniquely identifies one view definition for the list, which lets code or configuration point at that view.
levels.architect: It is an integer that uniquely identifies a view definition for a list. Do not confuse it with the [[list-identifier]], which identifies the list itself.

terms.summary: The base view identifier is the number that picks out one saved way of looking at a list.

levels.beginner: A basic page is a simple, plain page where one area can hold a piece of content.
levels.maker: It is a web parts page that has only one web part zone. By default it contains a Content Editor web part, so you can add text and images easily.
levels.architect: A basic page is a web parts page with a single zone. Its default content is a Content Editor web part, and any further [[web-part|web parts]] are added to that one zone.

terms.summary: A basic page is a simple, plain page where one area can hold a piece of content.

levels.beginner: BCS solution deployment is the process of getting a business-data solution from the server onto people's computers.
levels.maker: It is a way of deploying a server-side [[business-connectivity-services]] solution to client computers. It is based on ClickOnce technology, so the solution installs on the client.
levels.architect: The deployment is a server-to-client scenario that is based on ClickOnce. Plan for client machines to receive the solution through that mechanism.

terms.summary: BCS solution deployment is the process of getting a business-data solution from the server onto people's computers.

levels.beginner: A before event is a checkpoint that you must pass before the action can go ahead.
levels.maker: SharePoint raises it before an action runs. Its handler is synchronous and completes fully before the action that raised the event starts, which makes it useful when you want to check or change something first.
levels.architect: Before events are synchronous: the handler runs completely before the triggering action begins. That lets it validate or cancel the action, which an [[after-event]] cannot do.

terms.summary: A before event is a checkpoint that you must pass before the action can go ahead.

levels.beginner: A blank site is an empty room: a new site with nothing set up in it yet.
levels.maker: It is a site created from the Blank site template. Use it when you want to build the structure yourself rather than start from the lists and pages of something like a [[team-site]].
levels.architect: The site is created with the Blank template, so it starts with a minimal set of components. See [[site-template]] for how templates define a site.

terms.summary: A blank site is an empty room: a new site with nothing set up in it yet.

levels.beginner: Bring your own data means plugging your organisation's own information into an AI tool so its answers fit your business.
levels.maker: You choose which approved sources the experience may use, such as files, sites or a database, rather than relying on general knowledge alone.
levels.architect: Choose sources deliberately: each one widens what the AI can disclose. See [[knowledge-source]] and [[permission-trimming]] for how access is kept consistent with existing rights.

terms.summary: Bring your own data means plugging your organisation's own information into an AI tool so its answers fit your business.

levels.beginner: Browser context is the web page you are looking at, shared with an AI helper when you allow it.
levels.maker: Where a feature supports it, an assistant can use the current page or browsing session to answer questions about what you see.
levels.architect: Treat page content as untrusted input, since it may contain hidden instructions (see [[prompt-injection]]). Respect organisational policy on which pages may be shared.

terms.summary: Browser context is the web page you are looking at, shared with an AI helper when you allow it.

levels.beginner: Business Chat is an older name for the Copilot chat that could draw on your work information across apps.
levels.maker: You may still see the name in older articles and videos. Today's Microsoft 365 Copilot naming has moved on, so use [[microsoft-365-copilot-chat]] and [[microsoft-365-copilot]] for current terms.
levels.architect: When you meet the name in older documentation, map it to the cross-app chat experience in the current product, but check what the current product actually offers rather than assuming the features are identical.

terms.summary: Business Chat is an older name for the Copilot chat that could draw on your work information across apps.

levels.beginner: Business Connectivity Services lets you bring data from other business systems into SharePoint and Office, so people can use it without leaving those tools.
levels.maker: The feature lets users work with back-end line-of-business (LOB) data from inside the Office suite and SharePoint. It is known by several names, including BCS, Business Connectivity and Microsoft Business Connectivity Services.
levels.architect: BCS connects SharePoint and the Office suite to back-end data. A solution can be deployed to clients; see [[bcs-solution-deployment]]. Search for any of the variant names to land on this one concept.

terms.summary: Business Connectivity Services lets you bring data from other business systems into SharePoint and Office, so people can use it without leaving those tools.

levels.beginner: Business data is the information a company holds about its work: documents, emails, meetings, reports and records.
levels.maker: It gives AI answers something real to be based on. Without it the AI can only fall back on general knowledge.
levels.architect: It is the raw material for [[grounding]]. Access follows existing permissions, so poor permissions or labels on business data can lead to oversharing through AI.

terms.summary: Business data is the information a company holds about its work: documents, emails, meetings, reports and records.

levels.beginner: A business process is a repeatable set of steps that gets a job done, like approving an expense.
levels.maker: Copilot, agents, [[power-automate]] or [[copilot-studio]] can help with or automate parts of it. People usually still handle the judgement calls.
levels.architect: Map the process first, then decide which steps are retrieval, which are decisions and which are actions. Each automated step needs an owner, permissions and a way to handle exceptions.

terms.summary: A business process is a repeatable set of steps that gets a job done, like approving an expense.

levels.beginner: A business process flow is a guided path through a record, like a checklist across the top of a form that tells you which step comes next.
levels.maker: It makes sure people complete a record in the right order, for example moving a sales lead through its stages. It appears inside a [[model-driven-app]]. Despite the name it is not the same as a [[cloud-flow]], which runs automatically in the background.
levels.architect: A business process flow is defined on a [[dataverse-table]] as stages and steps, and it tracks progress against the record. It is authored in the Power Automate experience but evaluated in the app. Stages can require columns to be filled before a person moves on.

terms.summary: A business process flow is a guided path through a record, like a checklist across the top of a form that tells you which step comes next.

levels.beginner: A business system is a company's main working software, such as customer, finance or HR systems.
levels.maker: Copilot can be connected to these systems through approved integrations so it can read from them, and sometimes act in them.
levels.architect: Integration usually goes through a [[connector]], an API or a [[model-context-protocol|MCP]] server. Decide whether each connection is read-only and how the system's own security is respected.

terms.summary: A business system is a company's main working software, such as customer, finance or HR systems.

levels.beginner: CAML is a small XML language SharePoint uses to describe things like queries and views, a bit like a form with fixed boxes to fill in.
levels.maker: Collaborative Application Markup Language is an XML-based language that describes elements such as queries and views in sites built on SharePoint products and technologies. You will see it when a list view or a query is defined in a file.
levels.architect: CAML is XML, so queries and views are written as structured markup rather than as a general programming language. Many older customisations, view definitions and queries are expressed this way.

terms.summary: CAML is a small XML language SharePoint uses to describe things like queries and views, a bit like a form with fixed boxes to fill in.

levels.beginner: A canvas app is an app you design screen by screen, like arranging a poster: you place buttons, forms and pictures exactly where you want them.
levels.maker: You drag controls onto a screen and set how they behave with [[power-fx]] formulas. Canvas apps can read and write many data sources through [[connector|connectors]], so they suit tasks such as an approval form or an equipment check. If you would rather have the app built around your data, see [[model-driven-app]].
levels.architect: A canvas app is a set of screens made of controls bound to data sources. The maker decides layout, navigation and logic, so responsiveness and performance are the maker's job, and delegation limits matter for large data sources. Connections run with the signed-in user's permissions unless a shared connection is configured.

terms.summary: A canvas app is an app you design screen by screen, like arranging a poster: you place buttons, forms and pictures exactly where you want them.

levels.beginner: Central Administration is the control room of a SharePoint installation, where an administrator manages everything from one place.
levels.maker: It is a special SharePoint site used to manage all the sites and servers in a farm that runs SharePoint products and technologies. It belongs to the on-premises world, so SharePoint Online administrators use the admin centre instead.
levels.architect: Members of the [[farm-administrators-group]] use it for administrative tasks for the server or server farm. It is a farm-level tool on [[sharepoint-server]].

terms.summary: Central Administration is the control room of a SharePoint installation, where an administrator manages everything from one place.

levels.beginner: The chrome control draws the top bar of a page so that an add-in looks like it belongs inside SharePoint.
levels.maker: It is an HTML and JavaScript control that renders the top chrome and is available for use in apps for SharePoint, now called [[sharepoint-add-in|SharePoint Add-ins]]. It gives provider-hosted pages a familiar header.
levels.architect: The control is built with HTML and JavaScript, and it renders the top chrome for pages of an add-in. SharePoint Add-ins are retired in SharePoint Online and only remain for SharePoint Server, where this control can still be met.

terms.summary: The chrome control draws the top bar of a page so that an add-in looks like it belongs inside SharePoint.

levels.beginner: A citation is a pointer in an answer that shows where a statement came from, like a footnote.
levels.maker: Citations let you open the document or page behind a claim and check it. They make AI answers easier to trust and easier to correct.
levels.architect: They are only as good as the retrieval behind them, so a citation shows a source was used, not that the statement is correct. Use them as part of [[verification]] and to reduce [[hallucination]] risk.

terms.summary: A citation is a pointer in an answer that shows where a statement came from, like a footnote.

levels.beginner: A cloud flow is an automation that runs on Microsoft's servers, so it works even when your computer is off. Something starts it, such as a new email, a button press or a set time.
levels.maker: Cloud flows can start automatically when something changes, instantly when you select a button, or on a schedule. Each flow has a trigger followed by actions, and the steps use [[connector|connectors]]. A [[desktop-flow]] is the other main kind, for programs on a computer.
levels.architect: A cloud flow is a trigger plus actions, run by the Power Automate service under a connection. Retries, concurrency and run history are managed by the service. Include flows in a [[solution]] so they can be exported with their connection references and environment variables.

terms.summary: A cloud flow is an automation that runs on Microsoft's servers, so it works even when your computer is off. Something starts it, such as a new email, a button press or a set time.

levels.beginner: Column formatting changes how a column looks in a list or library, for example showing a status as a coloured label, without writing a program.
levels.maker: Open the column menu and choose to format the column, then start from a ready-made example or switch to advanced mode and edit the instructions. The same idea works for whole rows through view formatting. It only changes what people see: the data stays the same and the formatting does not hide anything from people who have access.
levels.architect: Formatting is a JSON description that follows a published schema: elements, styles and expressions that can read the current field and other fields, with Excel-style functions. It runs in the browser, so it is display-only and not a security control. When the JSON approach is not enough, a field customizer built with the [[spfx]] can render the column instead.

terms.summary: Column formatting changes how a column looks in a list or library, for example showing a status as a coloured label, without writing a program.

levels.beginner: A communication site is a SharePoint site for sharing information with many people, such as news, announcements and policies. It works like a company noticeboard or magazine: a few people write and many people read.
levels.maker: Communication sites are not connected to a Microsoft 365 group. A small set of owners and members author the pages, and a wide audience of visitors reads them. You start from a Topic, Showcase or Blank design. Use a [[team-site]] when everyone should work together on the content. Communication sites are often the starting point for a [[hub-site]] or the [[home-site]].
levels.architect: Created from the SITEPAGEPUBLISHING#0 template as the top-level site of its own [[site-collection]]. Permissions use the standard Owners, Members and Visitors SharePoint groups, so there is no group membership to sync. Pages are modern site pages built from [[web-part|web parts]].

terms.summary: A communication site is a SharePoint site for sharing information with many people, such as news, announcements and policies. It works like a company noticeboard or magazine: a few people write and many people read.

levels.beginner: A connector is a ready-made plug that lets an app or automation talk to another service, such as Outlook or SharePoint, without writing code.
levels.maker: Connectors wrap a service's API so you can use its data and actions from [[power-apps]], [[power-automate]] and [[copilot-studio]]. Some are standard and some are premium, and you can build custom ones. Administrators can control which connectors may be used together with [[data-policy|data policies]].
levels.architect: A connector is a strongly typed description of a REST API with its operations, triggers and authentication. A connection holds the credentials, and a connection reference lets a [[solution]] bind to a different connection in each [[environment]]. Custom connectors can wrap your own API through an OpenAPI definition.

terms.summary: A connector is a ready-made plug that lets an app or automation talk to another service, such as Outlook or SharePoint, without writing code.

levels.beginner: A content migration package is a box of files used to move content from one place to another.
levels.maker: It is a package of XML-formatted files used to migrate content between site collections, sites and lists. You use it when you need to copy or move structure and content rather than rebuild it.
levels.architect: The package is made of XML-formatted files. It supports moving content between [[site-collection|site collections]], sites and lists. A [[schema-version]] in the package identifies the version of its schema.

terms.summary: A content migration package is a box of files used to move content from one place to another.

levels.beginner: A content placeholder is an empty spot on a page template that gets filled in with the real content.
levels.maker: It is a region in a page layout that is filled dynamically with the value of the publishing page field it is bound to. Authors change the field, and the placeholder displays it.
levels.architect: Each placeholder is bound to a field of the [[publishing-page]]. The layout stays the same and the placeholder shows the value of the bound field.

terms.summary: A content placeholder is an empty spot on a page template that gets filled in with the real content.

levels.beginner: A content type is a reusable template that says what information belongs with a kind of item or document. For example, every "Contract" always carries a customer name and an end date, wherever it is stored.
levels.maker: A content type bundles [[site-column|site columns]] and can include a document template. Add it to a [[document-library]] or [[sharepoint-list]] and every item of that type gets the same fields. Content types can inherit from a parent type, and an organisation can publish them to many sites from the content type gallery.
levels.architect: The content type ID encodes the inheritance chain, for example 0x0101 for Document. Site content types live in a [[site-collection]], and each list gets a local copy when the type is added. Changes made to the parent can be pushed down to the copies. Cross-site distribution uses content type publishing from the gallery.

terms.summary: A content type is a reusable template that says what information belongs with a kind of item or document. For example, every "Contract" always carries a customer name and an end date, wherever it is stored.

levels.beginner: A content type group is a labelled shelf where similar content types are kept together.
levels.maker: It is a named category used to organise [[content-type|content types]] that have a similar purpose. It makes a long list of content types easier to browse.
levels.architect: The group is only an organising name. It does not change how an individual [[content-type]] behaves.

terms.summary: A content type group is a labelled shelf where similar content types are kept together.

levels.beginner: A content type identifier is the unique code that tells SharePoint exactly which content type you mean.
levels.maker: It is the unique identifier assigned to a [[content-type]]. Code and configuration use it because the display name can be duplicated or changed.
levels.architect: Always address a content type by its identifier in code. The identifier is assigned to the content type and is what makes it uniquely identifiable.

terms.summary: A content type identifier is the unique code that tells SharePoint exactly which content type you mean.

levels.beginner: Content type order is the sequence in which content types are listed, like the order of items on a menu.
levels.maker: It is the sequence in which content types are displayed, for example when a person chooses what kind of item to create. Changing it changes what people see first.
levels.architect: The order is part of how the content types of a list or folder are presented. It affects the display only, not the definition of the [[content-type]].

terms.summary: Content type order is the sequence in which content types are listed, like the order of items on a menu.

levels.beginner: A content type resource folder is the drawer where a content type keeps its extra files.
levels.maker: It is a folder that stores the resource files associated with a [[content-type]], such as templates or other supporting files.
levels.architect: The folder holds resource files that belong to one content type. Keep the files with the content type so they travel with it.

terms.summary: A content type resource folder is the drawer where a content type keeps its extra files.

levels.beginner: A content type schema is the written blueprint of a content type: it spells out what the content type contains.
levels.maker: It is an XML definition that describes the contents of a [[content-type]]. Tools and code can read it to know which fields the content type has.
levels.architect: The schema is XML, which is why it is read and written by deployment tooling. It describes the contents of the [[content-type]] in a form that machines can process.

terms.summary: A content type schema is the written blueprint of a content type: it spells out what the content type contains.

levels.beginner: A content type specific view is a special way of showing a list for just one kind of item.
levels.maker: It is a view associated with a particular content type that is attached to a folder. People who open that folder see the view designed for that content type.
levels.architect: The view is tied to a [[content-type]] that is associated with a [[list-folder|folder]]. It is useful when different folders should show their items differently.

terms.summary: A content type specific view is a special way of showing a list for just one kind of item.

levels.beginner: Context is the background information given to an AI along with your question, so it can answer sensibly.
levels.maker: It can include your chat so far, files, instructions and facts retrieved from work data. Better context usually means a better answer.
levels.architect: The model only sees what fits in the [[context-window]]. Context is assembled from [[system-prompt|system instructions]], [[conversation-history]], retrieved content and the user's [[prompt]], so what you include and exclude shapes the result.

terms.summary: Context is the background information given to an AI along with your question, so it can answer sensibly.

levels.beginner: The context site is simply the site you are working in at the moment of the request.
levels.maker: It is the site that matches the context of the current request. Features that depend on "the current site" resolve it from the request.
levels.architect: Resolve the context site from the incoming request, not from a stored setting. It is the site that corresponds to the context of the current request.

terms.summary: The context site is simply the site you are working in at the moment of the request.

levels.beginner: A context type is a label that sorts an event handler into a group.
levels.maker: It is a GUID used as a classification for an event receiver. It tells SharePoint what kind of context the receiver belongs to.
levels.architect: The value is a GUID that classifies an event receiver. Use it only as the classification; it is not an identifier of the site or the list.

terms.summary: A context type is a label that sorts an event handler into a group.

levels.beginner: The context window is how much an AI can keep in mind at once, like the size of its desk.
levels.maker: If a conversation or document is too long, parts may be left out or summarised, which is why long chats can seem to forget early details.
levels.architect: The window is measured in [[token|tokens]] and covers instructions, history, retrieved passages and the reply. Design agents to retrieve only what is relevant rather than stuffing everything in.

terms.summary: The context window is how much an AI can keep in mind at once, like the size of its desk.

levels.beginner: A contextual search scope narrows a search to the place you are in, such as one site or one list.
levels.maker: It is a system-defined restriction that can be added to a query so that results come only from a specific site or list. People get results relevant to where they are searching from.
levels.architect: The scope is system-defined and optional. When it is added to a query it restricts results to items from a particular site or list.

terms.summary: A contextual search scope narrows a search to the place you are in, such as one site or one list.

levels.beginner: Conversation history is the earlier part of a chat, which the AI reads so follow-up questions make sense.
levels.maker: It lets you say "make that shorter" without repeating yourself. Saved history also lets you find old chats later, subject to the product and admin settings.
levels.architect: Histories may be retained for continuity, support or governance, so [[retention]] and audit settings matter. Within a conversation, history consumes the [[context-window]]. It differs from [[memory]], which persists preferences across sessions.

terms.summary: Conversation history is the earlier part of a chat, which the AI reads so follow-up questions make sense.

levels.beginner: Copilot is Microsoft's name for the AI helpers built into its products, from Word and Teams to Windows and Azure.
levels.maker: The name is used broadly, so check which Copilot someone means. [[microsoft-365-copilot]] works with work data in Microsoft 365 apps, while other Copilots have other scopes.
levels.architect: Treat "Copilot" as a brand family, not a single product. Capabilities, licensing and data handling differ per product, so always qualify the name.

terms.summary: Copilot is Microsoft's name for the AI helpers built into its products, from Word and Teams to Windows and Azure.

levels.beginner: The Copilot Control System is the collection of admin tools for keeping Copilot and agents safe, managed and measured.
levels.maker: It gathers security, management and measurement capabilities so administrators can govern how Copilot and agents are used in the organisation.
levels.architect: It is an umbrella for controls across data protection, management, and reporting, including things such as the [[copilot-dashboard]]. Check the current list of included capabilities, as it evolves.

terms.summary: The Copilot Control System is the collection of admin tools for keeping Copilot and agents safe, managed and measured.

levels.beginner: Copilot Credits are the units you spend when you use the more advanced, usage-billed parts of Copilot, a bit like top-up credit on a phone.
levels.maker: They pay for work that the user licence does not cover, such as [[cowork]], [[autopilot]] and agents built on the [[microsoft-copilot-harness]]. They are separate from the Microsoft 365 Copilot [[licence]], which is why you can need both.
levels.architect: Credits are a consumption model under [[usage-based-billing]], so costs follow volume. Estimate usage, set budgets and monitor spend per workload. Pricing and what is covered change, so confirm current terms.

terms.summary: Copilot Credits are the units you spend when you use the more advanced, usage-billed parts of Copilot, a bit like top-up credit on a phone.

levels.beginner: The Copilot Dashboard is a report that shows how much Copilot is being used and what difference it makes.
levels.maker: Leaders and admins use it to understand adoption, usage patterns and impact on work, using signals available in Microsoft 365.
levels.architect: It draws on workplace analytics from [[viva-insights]]. It complements the admin [[usage-report|usage reports]], which are more about activity than outcomes.

terms.summary: The Copilot Dashboard is a report that shows how much Copilot is being used and what difference it makes.

levels.beginner: Copilot in Excel is an AI helper inside spreadsheets that can explain numbers and write formulas for you.
levels.maker: You can ask it to analyse data, spot trends, build formulas or create summaries, which is useful when you are not sure which function to use.
levels.architect: It works on the data in the workbook and, where permitted, other work content. Check its output, since formulas and calculations from AI still need [[verification]]. Tidy tables help it considerably.

terms.summary: Copilot in Excel is an AI helper inside spreadsheets that can explain numbers and write formulas for you.

levels.beginner: Copilot in Outlook is an AI helper in your email that can draft replies and summarise long threads.
levels.maker: It helps write, tidy and shorten messages and catch up on busy conversations, and where supported it can help with calendar tasks.
levels.architect: It uses the mailbox and other content the user can access. Review drafts before sending, and keep sensitive-information rules in mind, as with any [[draft]] written by AI.

terms.summary: Copilot in Outlook is an AI helper in your email that can draft replies and summarise long threads.

levels.beginner: Copilot in PowerPoint is an AI helper that can build and polish slide decks from your ideas or documents.
levels.maker: Use it to create a first draft, reorganise slides, shorten text or write speaker notes. You still edit the story and check the facts.
levels.architect: It can use files the user has access to as source material. Brand, accuracy and licensing of images remain the author's responsibility.

terms.summary: Copilot in PowerPoint is an AI helper that can build and polish slide decks from your ideas or documents.

levels.beginner: Copilot in Teams is an AI helper for meetings and chats that can summarise what was said and list actions.
levels.maker: It helps you catch up on a conversation, find decisions and follow-ups, and produce a [[meeting-recap]].
levels.architect: Meeting features depend on transcripts or recordings being available and allowed by policy. See [[transcript]] and [[retention]] for how that content is handled.

terms.summary: Copilot in Teams is an AI helper for meetings and chats that can summarise what was said and list actions.

levels.beginner: Copilot in Word is an AI writing helper that can draft, rewrite and summarise documents for you.
levels.maker: You can ask it to write a first version, change the tone, compare drafts or turn notes into a structured document.
levels.architect: It can draw on other documents you point it to. Treat its output as a [[draft]]: check facts, names and anything that could be a [[hallucination]].

terms.summary: Copilot in Word is an AI writing helper that can draft, rewrite and summarise documents for you.

levels.beginner: A Copilot Notebook is a place where you collect the files and notes for one topic so the AI can focus only on them.
levels.maker: Gathering the material for a project in one spot means questions are answered from those sources, which keeps answers more focused than searching everything.
levels.architect: A notebook limits [[grounding]] to selected sources, but user permissions still apply to each item. It differs from [[copilot-pages]], which are for editing and sharing output.

terms.summary: A Copilot Notebook is a place where you collect the files and notes for one topic so the AI can focus only on them.

levels.beginner: Copilot Pages are shared pages where you keep the good bits of an AI chat and keep working on them with others.
levels.maker: A Page is a shared, editable canvas. Turn any Copilot response into a living document that your team can co-edit with Copilot still in the loop, instead of losing a useful answer in a long conversation.
levels.architect: Pages build on the same collaboration technology as [[loop-component|Loop components]], so content stays editable and can be shared. Sharing follows normal permissions.

terms.summary: Copilot Pages are shared pages where you keep the good bits of an AI chat and keep working on them with others.

levels.beginner: Copilot Studio is where you build AI assistants, called agents, with little or no code. You describe what you want, give the agent knowledge and tools, then put it where people already work.
levels.maker: It is a graphical, low-code studio for building and managing [[agent|agents]] and workflows, connected to your data through [[connector|connectors]]. You can publish agents to channels such as Microsoft Teams, websites and mobile apps. It was called Power Virtual Agents before the rename, and the Teams edition became Copilot Studio for Teams in November 2023.
levels.architect: An [[agent]] follows instructions, uses [[knowledge-source|knowledge sources]] and calls [[agent-action|actions]], and the [[orchestrator]] decides how to combine them. Classic agents were built from [[topic|topics]]. Agents live in an [[environment]], move between them with [[solution|solutions]], and are governed by [[data-policy|data policies]].

terms.summary: Copilot Studio is where you build AI assistants, called agents, with little or no code. You describe what you want, give the agent knowledge and tools, then put it where people already work.

levels.beginner: Cowork is a Copilot mode where you describe a whole job and the AI plans it, does the steps across your tools and hands back a finished result.
levels.maker: It is Copilot's agentic system for delegated work. You describe a multi-step task and Cowork plans the steps, runs them across your tools and returns the finished result. It can run on demand, on a schedule, or when an email or Teams message arrives. It has been generally available since 16 June 2026, and needs a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence plus usage-based [[copilot-credits]].
levels.architect: Cowork sits on the advanced, usage-billed side of [[everyday-ai-and-advanced-ai]], so cost follows how much work it runs, not just how many licensed users you have. As an example of [[agentic-ai]] it acts across tools, so review the actions it takes, the scope of access it has and the triggers you set up. Capabilities and availability may change; confirm in current documentation.

terms.summary: Cowork is a Copilot mode where you describe a whole job and the AI plans it, does the steps across your tools and hands back a finished result.

levels.beginner: The crawl log is the diary of the search robot, noting where it succeeded and where it ran into problems.
levels.maker: It is a set of properties that gives information about the result of crawling a display URL. It includes whether the crawl was successful, the content source it belongs to, and the level, message, time and identifier for any errors.
levels.architect: Use the log to troubleshoot why an item is missing from search. It records success or failure per display URL, the content source, and details of any error. See also [[crawl-queue]].

terms.summary: The crawl log is the diary of the search robot, noting where it succeeded and where it ran into problems.

levels.beginner: The crawl queue is the to-do list of things the search robot will visit next.
levels.maker: It is a data structure that stores the list of items to crawl next. It fills as the crawler discovers links from the [[start-address|start addresses]].
levels.architect: The queue is a data structure that stores the list of items waiting to be crawled. It differs from the [[crawl-log]], which records outcomes of crawls that already happened.

terms.summary: The crawl queue is the to-do list of things the search robot will visit next.

levels.beginner: A crawled property is a piece of information the search robot finds about an item, like the author name on a book cover.
levels.maker: It is a type of metadata that can be discovered during a crawl and applied to one or more items. You can map it to a managed property to make it searchable in a controlled way.
levels.architect: Crawled properties are discovered during a crawl and can be applied to several items. They become useful for queries and refiners once mapped to a managed property. See also [[metadata-index]].

terms.summary: A crawled property is a piece of information the search robot finds about an item, like the author name on a book cover.

levels.beginner: The cross-domain library lets a page from one website talk to SharePoint on another site without being blocked.
levels.maker: It is a JavaScript library available in apps for SharePoint ([[sharepoint-add-in|SharePoint Add-ins]]) that allows cross-domain client-level communication. It was one of the ways that an add-in page could call back into SharePoint.
levels.architect: The library is JavaScript that lets client code communicate across domains. It is part of the add-in model that has been retired in SharePoint Online, so it is relevant only for existing add-ins on SharePoint Server. The [[web-proxy]] is a related mechanism.

terms.summary: The cross-domain library lets a page from one website talk to SharePoint on another site without being blocked.

levels.beginner: A custom action is an extra menu item or ribbon button that a developer adds to a SharePoint page.
levels.maker: It is a drop-down menu item or ribbon component added to a site page. The [[app-custom-action]] is the version that comes from an add-in, and modern pages use [[spfx]] extensions instead.
levels.architect: Custom actions add commands to menus and the ribbon of a page. Check the [[spfx]] extensions for the modern way to add commands to modern pages.

terms.summary: A custom action is an extra menu item or ribbon button that a developer adds to a SharePoint page.

levels.beginner: A custom engine agent is an assistant whose builders bring their own 'brain', the software and AI model that decide what to do, instead of using Copilot's.
levels.maker: It has its own orchestration logic and, optionally, its own model, and is built in [[copilot-studio]] or Microsoft Foundry. You choose the orchestrator and the models, which gives full control and is more power and more responsibility than a [[declarative-agent]]. It can still appear in Microsoft 365 places such as Teams. Pick it when a declarative agent isn't enough: a specific model, a special workflow or strict control over how responses are made.
levels.architect: You host the orchestration and model calls yourself, and take on the engineering that [[declarative-agent|declarative agents]] hand to the platform: prompts, grounding, evaluation, security and cost. Use this route when the managed [[orchestrator]] cannot meet your requirements. In Copilot Studio the engine underneath an agent is called a [[harness]], which also decides how it is billed.

terms.summary: A custom engine agent is an assistant whose builders bring their own 'brain', the software and AI model that decide what to do, instead of using Copilot's.

levels.beginner: The Customer Conversation harness is the engine for agents that talk to your customers, not your staff.
levels.maker: It supports customer-facing agents over web chat or a phone number, with escalation to a human representative when needed. It is billed in [[copilot-credits]] based on usage.
levels.architect: Design the [[handoff]] to a person carefully, including what context is passed on. Because customers, not employees, are the audience, review [[guardrail|guardrails]], [[moderation]] and data handling before going live.

terms.summary: The Customer Conversation harness is the engine for agents that talk to your customers, not your staff.

levels.beginner: A data boundary is a line around where your organisation's data may be stored and processed, like a country border for information.
levels.maker: Boundaries can be geographic, tenant-based or service-based. They matter to organisations with rules about where data may go, and they shape which AI features can be used.
levels.architect: Boundaries are defined by Microsoft service commitments and tenant configuration. Check how each Copilot feature, including any that call external services or models, is covered before relying on a boundary for compliance.

terms.summary: A data boundary is a line around where your organisation's data may be stored and processed, like a country border for information.

levels.beginner: Data loss prevention is a set of rules that stop sensitive information being shared where it should not be.
levels.maker: Admins define policies that spot things like card numbers or labelled files and then block, warn or log the sharing. They help limit what leaves the organisation, including through AI tools.
levels.architect: In Microsoft 365 DLP policies are managed in [[microsoft-purview]] and can use [[sensitivity-label|sensitivity labels]]. Test policies in audit mode first to avoid disrupting legitimate work.

terms.summary: Data loss prevention is a set of rules that stop sensitive information being shared where it should not be.

levels.beginner: Data minimisation means using only the information you really need for the job, and no more.
levels.maker: When connecting AI to data, choose the narrowest set of sources that does the task. That reduces risk if something goes wrong.
levels.architect: It is a privacy principle that complements [[least-privilege]]: limit what is collected and exposed, then limit who and what can reach it.

terms.summary: Data minimisation means using only the information you really need for the job, and no more.

levels.beginner: A data policy is a safety rule set by administrators that decides which services your apps and flows are allowed to connect with.
levels.maker: Administrators sort [[connector|connectors]] into groups or block them, so makers cannot combine a company data source with a personal one by mistake. Data policies used to be called data loss prevention (DLP) policies, so older material uses that name.
levels.architect: Data policies are set in the [[power-platform-admin-center]] at tenant or [[environment]] level and act as guardrails across Power Apps, Power Automate and Copilot Studio. A resource that breaks a policy can be blocked, so test policy changes before applying them widely.

terms.summary: A data policy is a safety rule set by administrators that decides which services your apps and flows are allowed to connect with.

levels.beginner: A data source is any place an AI helper can look things up, such as SharePoint, email or a database.
levels.maker: Admins and builders decide which data sources are available. The more sources, the more the AI can answer, and the more care you need over access.
levels.architect: Sources may be Microsoft 365 services, websites or external systems reached by a [[connector]] or [[graph-connector]]. In an agent, the chosen ones are configured as [[knowledge-source|knowledge sources]].

terms.summary: A data source is any place an AI helper can look things up, such as SharePoint, email or a database.

levels.beginner: The Data View web part is a window on a page that shows the items of a list.
levels.maker: It is a [[web-part]] used to display items in a list. It is related to, but not the same as, the [[list-view-web-part]], which generates HTML-based views of list items.
levels.architect: Treat it as one of the family of list-display web parts. Compare it with the [[list-view-web-part]] when choosing how to show list data.

terms.summary: The Data View web part is a window on a page that shows the items of a list.

levels.beginner: Dataverse is the place where Power Platform apps keep their data, in organised tables with built-in security. Think of it as a secure, well-labelled filing room.
levels.maker: Dataverse holds tables of data plus the rules around them, such as who may see what. [[model-driven-app|Model-driven apps]] require it, and it can also serve canvas apps, flows, agents and [[power-pages|Power Pages]] sites. It is not the same as a [[sharepoint-list]]: Dataverse is designed for structured business data with relationships and row-level security. It used to be called Common Data Service.
levels.architect: Dataverse is more than a database: it also provides web services (the Web API and the SDK), relationships, business logic and role-based security inside an [[environment]]. Developers see different words for the same things, for example a table is an entity and a column is an attribute in the SDK. See [[dataverse-table]].

terms.summary: Dataverse is the place where Power Platform apps keep their data, in organised tables with built-in security. Think of it as a secure, well-labelled filing room.

levels.beginner: A choice is a column that lets people pick from a fixed list, like a drop-down for status: Open, In progress, Done.
levels.maker: Choices keep answers consistent, so reports can count them reliably. Power Apps screens call them choices, while developers meet them as option sets. A yes/no column is a related, simpler type.
levels.architect: A choice appears as an OptionSet or Picklist in the SDK and an OptionSet in the Web API. Each option has a numeric value and a label, and the value is what is stored, which lets labels be translated. Choices can be shared across tables when they are defined globally.

terms.summary: A choice is a column that lets people pick from a fixed list, like a drop-down for status: Open, In progress, Done.

levels.beginner: A column is one detail you record about every row in a table, such as a customer's email address or an order's due date.
levels.maker: Columns have types such as text, number, date or choice, and some can be required. A column used to be called a field. Developers call the same thing an attribute.
levels.architect: The same idea is a column in the Power Apps screens, an Attribute in the SDK and a Property in the Web API. Changing a column's type later can be restricted, so choose types deliberately. Dependencies matter: a [[model-driven-view|view]] that shows a column needs it to exist.

terms.summary: A column is one detail you record about every row in a table, such as a customer's email address or an order's due date.

levels.beginner: A row is a single entry in a table, such as one customer. It holds the values of every column for that one thing.
levels.maker: Power Apps screens say row, while developer tools and many older articles say record. A [[sharepoint-list]] calls the same idea an item.
levels.architect: In the SDK a row is a record, an instance of the Entity class, and in the Web API you create one by POSTing data shaped like the table's EntityType. Access to rows is governed by [[security-role|security roles]] and ownership.

terms.summary: A row is a single entry in a table, such as one customer. It holds the values of every column for that one thing.

levels.beginner: A Dataverse table is like a spreadsheet tab for one kind of thing, such as customers or orders. Each row is one customer, and each column is one detail about them.
levels.maker: Tables hold your rows, and you can relate them, for example one customer to many orders. Power Apps screens say table, while older articles and developer tools say entity. It looks similar to a [[sharepoint-list]], but a Dataverse table has relationships, business rules and fine-grained security built in.
levels.architect: In the Dataverse SDK a table is an Entity with an Attributes collection, and in the Web API it is an EntityType with properties, following OData terminology. Use the table designer to build tables and [[solution|solutions]] to move their definitions. Tables carry [[dataverse-column|columns]], relationships and [[security-role|security role]] privileges.

terms.summary: A Dataverse table is like a spreadsheet tab for one kind of thing, such as customers or orders. Each row is one customer, and each column is one detail about them.

levels.beginner: A declarative agent is a version of Copilot that you set up for one purpose by writing instructions and choosing what it can look at and do. You do not build the thinking part yourself.
levels.maker: It is defined by configuration, not code: instructions, [[knowledge-source|knowledge sources]] and starter prompts, plus any [[agent-action|actions]]. It is what you build in [[agent-builder]], and the simpler option in [[copilot-studio]]. Microsoft 365 Copilot's own orchestrator and models do the reasoning. It is the quicker route and suits most scenarios. If you need your own orchestrator or models, see [[custom-engine-agent]].
levels.architect: Declarative agents run on Microsoft 365 Copilot's managed orchestration and language-model infrastructure. You configure the agent in a manifest instead of hosting a conversational runtime, so you cannot replace the orchestrator with your own code. Which capabilities are available depends on the authoring tool, manifest version, target experience, licensing and policies. Ready-made agents from Microsoft are covered under [[first-party-agents]].

terms.summary: A declarative agent is a version of Copilot that you set up for one purpose by writing instructions and choosing what it can look at and do. You do not build the thinking part yourself.

levels.beginner: A declarative workflow association connects a no-code workflow to the list or content type it should run on.
levels.maker: It is a code-free binding of a declarative workflow to a specific list or content type, using XAML (Extensible Application Markup Language). It is a kind of [[workflow-association]].
levels.architect: The binding is made with XAML and does not need custom code. See [[workflow-association]] for the general idea of attaching a workflow template to a list or [[content-type]].

terms.summary: A declarative workflow association connects a no-code workflow to the list or content type it should run on.

levels.beginner: Deep research is when an AI spends longer digging through many sources and then writes a thorough report, instead of giving a quick reply.
levels.maker: It is slower than an ordinary chat answer but can give more developed results with sources. Use it for questions that need real investigation.
levels.architect: It typically plans queries, retrieves from many sources, reasons over findings and assembles a report with references. Check the sources it cites, as quality depends on what it could reach.

terms.summary: Deep research is when an AI spends longer digging through many sources and then writes a thorough report, instead of giving a quick reply.

levels.beginner: The default list view is the way a list looks when you open it without choosing anything special.
levels.maker: It is the view of a [[sharepoint-list]] that the list owner defines to appear when people browse to the list without specifying a view. Pick it with care, because most visitors only ever see that view.
levels.architect: The owner of the list defines which view acts as the default. Mobile browsing has its own equivalent, the [[default-mobile-list-view]].

terms.summary: The default list view is the way a list looks when you open it without choosing anything special.

levels.beginner: The default mobile list view is the way a list looks on a phone or tablet when no other view is chosen.
levels.maker: It is the view of a list that the owner defines to appear when people browse to the list from a mobile device without specifying a view. It lets mobile visitors see a simpler layout than the normal [[default-list-view]].
levels.architect: The list owner defines it separately from the [[default-list-view]], so the desktop and mobile experiences can differ.

terms.summary: The default mobile list view is the way a list looks on a phone or tablet when no other view is chosen.

levels.beginner: The default search scope is the search area used automatically if nobody picks another one.
levels.maker: It is the search scope that is assigned automatically to a search scope display group. Searches in that group use it unless the person chooses a different one.
