levels.maker: Solutions hold apps, flows, tables, security roles and more. They come in two types: unmanaged, which you can still edit, and managed, which is locked for the people who install it. Putting your work in a solution is how you share it and keep it organised.
levels.architect: Solutions are the mechanism for application lifecycle management across Power Platform. Every solution has a publisher whose prefix names its components, and solutions can depend on one another. Develop in unmanaged form in a development [[environment]], then export as managed for test and production, ideally through an automated pipeline.

terms.summary: A solution is a box that you pack your apps and flows into so you can carry them from one environment to another.

levels.beginner: A source is the document, page or record that an answer was based on.
levels.maker: Seeing sources lets you check the answer.
levels.architect: Source quality, access and recency decide answer reliability.

terms.summary: A source is the document, page or record that an answer was based on.

levels.beginner: Speech-to-text turns spoken words into written text.
levels.maker: It powers transcripts and voice prompts.
levels.architect: Accuracy depends on audio quality, accents and domain words.

terms.summary: Speech-to-text turns spoken words into written text.

levels.beginner: The standard harness is the engine for agents that follow the conversation paths and rules that you write, so they behave predictably.
levels.maker: It runs the [[topic|topics]] and rules you author, which makes conversations structured and repeatable. Its usage is covered for employees who have a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence and use it under their own identity. Unlicensed users, autonomous runs and computer use are still billed.
levels.architect: Check the cost for each case rather than assuming the licence covers everything: coverage depends on whose identity is used and whether the run is autonomous. See the [[microsoft-copilot-harness]] for the fully usage-billed alternative.

terms.summary: The standard harness is the engine for agents that follow the conversation paths and rules that you write, so they behave predictably.

levels.beginner: A start address is the web address where the search robot begins.
levels.maker: It is a URL that identifies a point at which to start a crawl. Administrators specify start addresses when they create or edit a content source.
levels.architect: The crawl begins at the address given for a content source. Items found from it join the [[crawl-queue]].

terms.summary: A start address is the web address where the search robot begins.

levels.beginner: Static rank is how important search thinks an item is, independent of what you typed.
levels.maker: It is the component of a rank that does not depend on the search query. It represents the perceived importance of an item and can relate to its origin, to the relationships between the item and other items, or to business rules defined in the search application.
levels.architect: It does not change with the query, unlike [[dynamic-rank]]. Business rules from the search application can feed into it.

terms.summary: Static rank is how important search thinks an item is, independent of what you typed.

levels.beginner: Summarisation is shortening a long thing into its main points.
levels.maker: It works for documents, emails, meetings and chats.
levels.architect: Summaries can drop or distort details, so check anything important.

terms.summary: Summarisation is shortening a long thing into its main points.

levels.beginner: Supervised learning is teaching a model with examples that come with the right answers.
levels.maker: It learns by comparing its guesses with the known answers.
levels.architect: Needs labelled data. Contrast with unsupervised or self-supervised training.

terms.summary: Supervised learning is teaching a model with examples that come with the right answers.

levels.beginner: Synthetic data is made-up data that looks like the real thing.
levels.maker: It is handy for testing without using real customer or staff records.
levels.architect: Check that it is realistic enough and doesn't leak real records.

terms.summary: Synthetic data is made-up data that looks like the real thing.

levels.beginner: A system prompt is the hidden set of rules an AI app gives the model before your question.
levels.maker: It sets the role, tone and limits of the assistant.
levels.architect: It has higher priority than the user prompt but can still be attacked, see [[prompt-injection]].

terms.summary: A system prompt is the hidden set of rules an AI app gives the model before your question.

levels.beginner: A task is one job you ask Copilot or an agent to do, from a quick summary to a whole process.
levels.maker: Clear tasks with a clear finish line give better results.
levels.architect: Define success criteria for each task so it can be checked in [[evaluation]].

terms.summary: A task is one job you ask Copilot or an agent to do, from a quick summary to a whole process.

levels.beginner: Task orchestration is arranging several steps, tools and data lookups in the right order to reach a bigger goal.
levels.maker: It is how an agent handles a multi-step request.
levels.architect: It is the sequencing part of [[orchestration]]; handle failures and retries explicitly.

terms.summary: Task orchestration is arranging several steps, tools and data lookups in the right order to reach a bigger goal.

levels.beginner: A team site is a SharePoint site built for people who work together on a project or in a department. It is the team's shared workspace for files, tasks and news, where everyone on the team can add and edit.
levels.maker: A team site is usually connected to a Microsoft 365 group, which also gives the team a shared mailbox and calendar and links it to Microsoft Teams and Planner. Members edit content freely. Choose a [[communication-site]] instead when a few people publish and many people read. A team site can also be created without a Microsoft 365 group.
levels.architect: Group-connected team sites are created from the GROUP#0 template, and the Microsoft 365 group's owners and members map to the site's Owners and Members. Visitors are managed separately in SharePoint. The non-group variant uses the STS#3 template and is managed through SharePoint groups only. Either way the site is the top-level site of its own [[site-collection]].

terms.summary: A team site is a SharePoint site built for people who work together on a project or in a department. It is the team's shared workspace for files, tasks and news, where everyone on the team can add and edit.

levels.beginner: Temperature is a dial for how adventurous an AI's wording is.
levels.maker: Lower values give steadier answers and higher values give more variety, where the product lets you change it.
levels.architect: Use low values for factual or structured work and higher ones for brainstorming.

terms.summary: Temperature is a dial for how adventurous an AI's wording is.

levels.beginner: A tenant is your organisation's own private space in Microsoft's cloud.
levels.maker: It holds your users, licences, policies, apps and data, separate from other organisations.
levels.architect: Settings such as policies and [[data-boundary|data boundaries]] are tenant-level, while an [[environment]] is a narrower container inside it.

terms.summary: A tenant is your organisation's own private space in Microsoft's cloud.

levels.beginner: Tenant data is everything stored in your organisation's Microsoft cloud tenant.
levels.maker: It includes content, settings, identities and service data, all subject to permissions.
levels.architect: Understand how Copilot features use and process it, within your [[data-boundary]].

terms.summary: Tenant data is everything stored in your organisation's Microsoft cloud tenant.

levels.beginner: The term store is a central list of agreed words, such as department names or product categories. People pick from it when they tag files, so everyone tags things the same way.
levels.maker: Admins build the list in the term store tool: terms live in term sets, and term sets live in groups. A managed metadata [[site-column]] points at a term set, so tagging gives a pick list instead of free typing. Terms can have synonyms and can be arranged in a hierarchy.
levels.architect: Terms have GUIDs, so renaming a term does not break the items tagged with it. In each site collection, tagged values are mirrored in a hidden taxonomy list, which is why a restored or copied item may need its tags re-linked. The service is tenant-wide in SharePoint Online and a service application in [[sharepoint-server]]. It is also available through Microsoft Graph.

terms.summary: The term store is a central list of agreed words, such as department names or product categories. People pick from it when they tag files, so everyone tags things the same way.

levels.beginner: A token is a small chunk of text, roughly a short word or part of one, that an AI reads and writes.
levels.maker: Limits and costs are often counted in tokens rather than words.
levels.architect: Context length, [[usage-based-billing|billing]] and [[latency]] depend on token counts. Do not confuse it with security tokens used in [[authentication]].

terms.summary: A token is a small chunk of text, roughly a short word or part of one, that an AI reads and writes.

levels.beginner: Tool calling is when an AI decides to use a tool, like a calculator or a search, to get something done.
levels.maker: The model does not do everything by itself. It asks for a defined function to run, such as "look up this order", and uses the result.
levels.architect: The model emits a structured request with parameters, and the system executes it and returns the result. Validate parameters, apply permissions and log calls, since the model's request is not automatically safe. See [[agent-action]] and [[model-context-protocol]].

terms.summary: Tool calling is when an AI decides to use a tool, like a calculator or a search, to get something done.

levels.beginner: A topic is one conversation an agent knows how to have, such as 'reset my password' or 'opening hours'.
levels.maker: In [[copilot-studio]], a topic holds the steps of a conversation about one subject and starts when a user says something that matches. Agents can combine topics with [[knowledge-source|knowledge]] and [[agent-action|actions]]. Topics were the main building block of Power Virtual Agents.
levels.architect: A topic defines how it is triggered and then a series of steps that ask questions, set variables, call actions and send messages. Agents that use generative orchestration can choose among topics, tools and knowledge dynamically, so give topics clear names and descriptions, because the [[orchestrator]] relies on them.

terms.summary: A topic is one conversation an agent knows how to have, such as 'reset my password' or 'opening hours'.

levels.beginner: A trace is a step-by-step record of how an agent handled a request.
levels.maker: It shows tool calls and decisions, which helps when something goes wrong.
levels.architect: Traces may contain sensitive data, so control access and retention.

terms.summary: A trace is a step-by-step record of how an agent handled a request.

levels.beginner: A transcript is a written copy of what was said in a conversation or meeting.
levels.maker: Copilot can use transcripts of supported Teams meetings to summarise and answer questions.
levels.architect: Transcription must be enabled and permitted. See [[retention]].

terms.summary: A transcript is a written copy of what was said in a conversation or meeting.

levels.beginner: Trusted authentication lets one account act on behalf of the person who is currently signed in.
levels.maker: It is a mechanism whereby a user account or a process account can be used to perform operations on behalf of the current user.
levels.architect: An account is trusted to perform operations for the current user. It is different from a [[trusted-subsystem]], which is a two-way trust between server components.

terms.summary: Trusted authentication lets one account act on behalf of the person who is currently signed in.

levels.beginner: A trusted subsystem is a pair of servers that trust each other to do privileged jobs.
levels.maker: It is a method of communication in which two-way trust is established between two server components. Each uses an account authorised to perform privileged actions such as retrieving files and settings.
levels.architect: Each component talks to the other using an account that is authorised for privileged actions. Compare with [[trusted-authentication]].

terms.summary: A trusted subsystem is a pair of servers that trust each other to do privileged jobs.

levels.beginner: The UI culture is the language that a screen uses to talk to you.
levels.maker: It is the language used to display strings and other graphical elements in a user interface.
levels.architect: Choose it separately from the data formats that a person might expect.

terms.summary: The UI culture is the language that a screen uses to talk to you.

levels.beginner: The unified audit log is a central record of activity across Microsoft services.
levels.maker: It is used for investigations, governance and compliance.
levels.architect: It is a [[microsoft-purview]] audit source; check which Copilot activity is recorded and for how long.

terms.summary: The unified audit log is a central record of activity across Microsoft services.

levels.beginner: Unstructured data is information that doesn't fit neat rows and columns, like documents, emails and chats.
levels.maker: Most workplace content is of this kind, which is why AI is useful for it.
levels.architect: It needs retrieval and language models rather than simple queries.

terms.summary: Unstructured data is information that doesn't fit neat rows and columns, like documents, emails and chats.

levels.beginner: Uploading is giving a file straight to the AI.
levels.maker: The file can be used as reference material, temporarily or more permanently depending on the product.
levels.architect: Check where uploaded files are stored and for how long.

terms.summary: Uploading is giving a file straight to the AI.

levels.beginner: A usage report shows how much Copilot and agents are used.
levels.maker: Admins use these to see adoption and activity.
levels.architect: Reports describe activity, not business value, and data may lag.

terms.summary: A usage report shows how much Copilot and agents are used.

levels.beginner: Usage-based billing means you pay for what you use rather than a flat fee.
levels.maker: For some agents and Copilot features, charges depend on how much they are used. In Copilot this is measured in [[copilot-credits]], and it covers the advanced, long-running work described in [[everyday-ai-and-advanced-ai]], such as [[cowork]] and [[autopilot]], while the user licence covers everyday use.
levels.architect: Estimate volume, set budgets and monitor consumption. Coverage differs by workload and engine: for example the [[microsoft-copilot-harness]] bills credits for all usage, while the [[standard-harness]] is covered for licensed employees using it under their own identity. Pricing changes, so check current documentation.

terms.summary: Usage-based billing means you pay for what you use rather than a flat fee.

levels.beginner: User context is what is known about the person asking: who they are, their role, files and activity.
levels.maker: It lets answers fit the individual.
levels.architect: Bound by permissions and privacy settings.

terms.summary: User context is what is known about the person asking: who they are, their role, files and activity.

levels.beginner: A user display name is the name a person prefers to be shown as.
levels.maker: It is a user profile property that can contain the preferred name of a user. It is stored in the [[user-profile-store]].
levels.architect: It is a profile property in the [[user-profile-store]] and holds the preferred name.

terms.summary: A user display name is the name a person prefers to be shown as.

levels.beginner: User grounding is the AI using information about you to make an answer fit your work.
levels.maker: It is only information you are allowed to access.
levels.architect: Respects [[permission-trimming]].

terms.summary: User grounding is the AI using information about you to make an answer fit your work.

levels.beginner: User permissions are the access rights a person has.
levels.maker: Copilot acting for you can only reach what your permissions allow.
levels.architect: Review over-sharing before deploying Copilot widely.

terms.summary: User permissions are the access rights a person has.

levels.beginner: The user profile change entry log is the diary of every change made to profiles.
levels.maker: It is a repository that logs all the changes that take place in a user profile. Each change is a [[user-profile-change-event]].
levels.architect: The log holds a record of all the changes to profiles in the [[user-profile-store]].

terms.summary: The user profile change entry log is the diary of every change made to profiles.

levels.beginner: A user profile change event is the moment when something on a profile changes.
levels.maker: It is an event that occurs when a property of any user profile is changed. It is logged in the [[user-profile-change-entry-log]].
levels.architect: The event fires on a change to any property of any profile.

terms.summary: A user profile change event is the moment when something on a profile changes.

levels.beginner: A user profile import is the process of bringing people's details in from the company directory.
levels.maker: It is the process of importing records from a directory service to the [[user-profile-store]].
levels.architect: Records come from a directory service and go into the [[user-profile-store]].

terms.summary: A user profile import is the process of bringing people's details in from the company directory.

levels.beginner: It is the unique number of one profile record.
levels.maker: It is an integer that uniquely identifies a user profile record in the [[user-profile-store]].
levels.architect: The integer identifies a single record in the profile store.

terms.summary: It is the unique number of one profile record.

levels.beginner: The user profile store is the database that keeps everyone's profile details.
levels.maker: It is a database that stores information about each user profile. Imports fill it, see [[user-profile-import]].
levels.architect: Profile data, such as the [[user-display-name]], is kept here.

terms.summary: The user profile store is the database that keeps everyone's profile details.

levels.beginner: The user search security filter is a list of what each person may see, applied to search results so that people never see things they should not.
levels.maker: It specifies the group and user permissions for a specific FAST Search user. FAST Search Authorization (FSA) intersects the user's query with the filter and checks each document's access control list. It is the main way FSA enforces document-level security, also called security trimming.
levels.architect: FSA filters out inappropriate results by intersecting the query with the filter and checking each document's [[access-control-list]]. The [[public-filter]] covers documents everyone can see.

terms.summary: The user search security filter is a list of what each person may see, applied to search results so that people never see things they should not.

levels.beginner: A user store is a list of people, groups and their rights that belongs to another security system.
levels.maker: It is a logical grouping of users, groups and content permissions for a third-party security or content system that FAST Search Authorization accesses.
levels.architect: The store belongs to a third-party system. See [[default-user-store]] and [[principal-aliasing]].

terms.summary: A user store is a list of people, groups and their rights that belongs to another security system.

levels.beginner: A variable is a named box that holds a value for later, such as what the user typed.
levels.maker: Agents and workflows use them to remember inputs and results from earlier steps.
levels.architect: Scope and lifetime matter: some are limited to a topic and some persist. Avoid storing secrets in them.

terms.summary: A variable is a named box that holds a value for later, such as what the user typed.

levels.beginner: A vector is a list of numbers that stands for the meaning of something.
levels.maker: Computers compare vectors to tell how similar two things are.
levels.architect: Vectors from the same model can be compared with measures such as cosine similarity.

terms.summary: A vector is a list of numbers that stands for the meaning of something.

levels.beginner: A vector database stores those number lists so similar things can be found quickly.
levels.maker: It is common behind AI search and retrieval.
levels.architect: Evaluate access control, scale and update behaviour.

terms.summary: A vector database stores those number lists so similar things can be found quickly.

levels.beginner: Vector search finds content whose meaning is close to your question.
levels.maker: It matches ideas, not just words.
levels.architect: Often combined with [[keyword-search]] in [[hybrid-search]].

terms.summary: Vector search finds content whose meaning is close to your question.

levels.beginner: Verification is checking an AI answer against something reliable before you use it.
levels.maker: It matters most for numbers, quotes, legal or financial content.
levels.architect: Use sources, calculation checks and expert review; automate checks where possible.

terms.summary: Verification is checking an AI answer against something reliable before you use it.

levels.beginner: Version history keeps earlier copies of a file or list item every time it is saved, so you can look back at changes or bring an older version back.
levels.maker: In a [[document-library]] you open the version history of a file, see who changed it and when, and restore or view an earlier version. By default libraries keep major versions up to a limit that site owners and admins can change. Version history is for changes to something that still exists. A deleted item goes to the [[recycle-bin]] instead.
levels.architect: Every saved version counts toward the site's storage, so unlimited versions of large files grow quickly. SharePoint can trim old versions automatically within the limits you set. Versioning is not a backup: it does not protect against the whole site or library being lost, which is what a service such as [[microsoft-365-backup]] is for.

terms.summary: Version history keeps earlier copies of a file or list item every time it is saved, so you can look back at changes or bring an older version back.

levels.beginner: A view is a saved way of looking at a list of rows, with chosen columns and filters, like a filtered spreadsheet you can reopen.
levels.maker: A table can have many views, such as 'My open cases'. Views can be filtered in advance, and the app decides which views to offer. A SharePoint library has views too, so the idea will feel familiar if you know a [[document-library]].
levels.architect: A view is a stored query plus a layout on a [[dataverse-table]]. It depends on the columns it shows, so removing a column that a view uses is blocked until the view changes. Ship views in a [[solution]].

terms.summary: A view is a saved way of looking at a list of rows, with chosen columns and filters, like a filtered spreadsheet you can reopen.

levels.beginner: A visible scope is a search area that people can actually see and choose.
levels.maker: It is a search scope that is displayed to site collection administrators and users.
levels.architect: Only visible scopes are displayed. See [[search-scope-display-group]] for how scopes are grouped.

terms.summary: A visible scope is a search area that people can actually see and choose.

levels.beginner: The Visitors group is the standard group for people who may look but not change things.
levels.maker: It is a default group of users on a SharePoint site. By default the Visitors group is assigned the Read permission level. See [[sharepoint-groups]].
levels.architect: The default permission level is Read. The [[members-group]] has Contribute by default.

terms.summary: The Visitors group is the standard group for people who may look but not change things.

levels.beginner: Viva Engage is Microsoft's social network for organisations, where people share updates and join communities.
levels.maker: It used to be called Yammer, and the old name still turns up in older documents and conversations.
levels.architect: When searching documentation, try both names, since older material uses Yammer.

terms.summary: Viva Engage is Microsoft's social network for organisations, where people share updates and join communities.

levels.beginner: Viva Insights is Microsoft's service about how people work, including collaboration patterns and wellbeing.
levels.maker: It also supplies reporting used to understand Copilot adoption.
levels.architect: Review privacy settings and aggregation rules.

terms.summary: Viva Insights is Microsoft's service about how people work, including collaboration patterns and wellbeing.

levels.beginner: Voice input means speaking your request instead of typing.
levels.maker: Where supported, it makes Copilot easier to use hands-free.
levels.architect: Depends on [[speech-to-text]]. Consider privacy in shared spaces.

terms.summary: Voice input means speaking your request instead of typing.

levels.beginner: A web application identifier is the unique code of a web application.
levels.maker: It is a GUID that identifies a web application.
levels.architect: The GUID identifies the web application, which sits above the [[site-collection]] level.

terms.summary: A web application identifier is the unique code of a web application.

levels.beginner: A web control is a reusable building block on the server that draws part of a page.
levels.maker: It is a server-side component that encapsulates user interface and related functionality. It is not the same as a [[web-part]].
levels.architect: The component runs on the server. Its server-side nature makes it a farm-era technique.

terms.summary: A web control is a reusable building block on the server that draws part of a page.

levels.beginner: Web data is information from public web pages given to the AI as context.
levels.maker: It adds current information beyond your organisation's content.
levels.architect: Quality varies; treat as untrusted and cite it.

terms.summary: Web data is information from public web pages given to the AI as context.

levels.beginner: A web discussion comment is a single note added to a web discussion.
levels.maker: It is an individual comment that is added within a web discussion.
levels.architect: Each comment is one entry inside a web discussion.

terms.summary: A web discussion comment is a single note added to a web discussion.

levels.beginner: Web grounding lets the AI check the internet for current information when answering.
levels.maker: It helps with recent events and public facts.
levels.architect: Admins may control it. Queries sent to web search may leave the organisation's boundary, so check the settings.

terms.summary: Web grounding lets the AI check the internet for current information when answering.

levels.beginner: A web part is a building block you place on a SharePoint page, such as a text box, an image gallery, a news feed or a list of documents. You build a page by stacking web parts.
levels.maker: On modern pages you add web parts from the plus button in the page editor. SharePoint ships many, for example News, Highlighted content and Quick links. Developers can add their own with the [[spfx]]. Older classic web parts belong to classic pages.
levels.architect: Modern web parts are client-side components, built with the [[spfx]] and configured through a property pane. Classic web parts are server-side and are defined by Web Part Gallery entries and .webpart files, and they do not run on modern pages. Moving to modern means replacing them with modern or SPFx equivalents.

terms.summary: A web part is a building block you place on a SharePoint page, such as a text box, an image gallery, a news feed or a list of documents. You build a page by stacking web parts.

levels.beginner: The web part cache is a quick-reference list that web parts use to look up information fast.
levels.maker: It is a hash table of key and value pairs that is used to cache and locate internal information for [[web-part|web parts]].
levels.architect: It is a hash table of key and value pairs holding internal information of web parts.

terms.summary: The web part cache is a quick-reference list that web parts use to look up information fast.

levels.beginner: The chrome state says whether a web part is shown open or collapsed.
levels.maker: It is the condition of a [[web-part]] and the chrome around it. The possible values are zero (0) for normal state and one (1) for minimised state.
levels.architect: Zero means normal and one means minimised.

terms.summary: The chrome state says whether a web part is shown open or collapsed.

levels.beginner: A web part connection is a link between two web parts so one can pass data to the other.
levels.maker: It is an element in a web parts page that defines a provider and consumer data relationship between two [[web-part|web parts]]. Data from one can change what and how the other is rendered.
levels.architect: One part provides data and the other consumes it when the page is rendered.

terms.summary: A web part connection is a link between two web parts so one can pass data to the other.

levels.beginner: A web part identifier is the unique code of one web part on a page.
levels.maker: It is a GUID that identifies a [[web-part]]. It differs from the [[web-part-type-identifier]].
levels.architect: The GUID names the part. The type identifier names the kind.

terms.summary: A web part identifier is the unique code of one web part on a page.

levels.beginner: A web part property is a setting that changes how a web part behaves.
levels.maker: It is a configurable characteristic of a [[web-part]] that determines its behaviour.
levels.architect: Properties are configurable and determine the behaviour of the part.

terms.summary: A web part property is a setting that changes how a web part behaves.

levels.beginner: A web part type identifier is the unique code of a kind of web part.
levels.maker: It is a unique 16-byte value that is assigned to each web part type. See [[web-part-identifier]].
levels.architect: The value is 16 bytes long and assigned to each type of [[web-part]].

terms.summary: A web part type identifier is the unique code of a kind of web part.

levels.beginner: It is the name tag of an area on a page where web parts can be placed.
levels.maker: It is a string that identifies a web part zone on a web parts page.
levels.architect: The string names the zone. The [[web-part-zone-index]] orders parts within it.

terms.summary: It is the name tag of an area on a page where web parts can be placed.

levels.beginner: The zone index sets the order of web parts in the same area.
levels.maker: It is an integer that specifies the relative position of a web part in a web part zone. Web parts are positioned from the smallest to the largest index.
levels.architect: Two parts with the same index are placed next to each other in an undefined order.

terms.summary: The zone index sets the order of web parts in the same area.

levels.beginner: The web proxy is a go-between that lets SharePoint pass a request on to another service.
levels.maker: It is a method exposed in a client object model to issue requests from SharePoint to a remote service. Developers could use it in apps for SharePoint, now [[sharepoint-add-in|SharePoint Add-ins]].
levels.architect: The method belongs to the add-in model that is retired in SharePoint Online. Compare with the [[cross-domain-library]].

terms.summary: The web proxy is a go-between that lets SharePoint pass a request on to another service.

levels.beginner: Web search is looking things up on the internet.
levels.maker: It supplements the model's knowledge and your work data.
levels.architect: Review policy on web access for AI.

terms.summary: Web search is looking things up on the internet.

levels.beginner: A web service method is an action that a service offers, which other programs can ask for.
levels.maker: It is a procedure exposed to web service clients as an operation that can be called on the web service.
levels.architect: Clients call it as an operation of the service.

terms.summary: A web service method is an action that a service offers, which other programs can ask for.

levels.beginner: Whiteboard Copilot is AI help for brainstorming on a shared whiteboard.
levels.maker: It can help generate and group ideas.
levels.architect: Check what content the AI can see on the board.

terms.summary: Whiteboard Copilot is AI help for brainstorming on a shared whiteboard.

levels.beginner: Work IQ is Microsoft's way of giving Copilot and agents an understanding of how your work happens.
levels.maker: It brings together data, memory and inference so agents can use real organisational context.
levels.architect: It is described in layers: [[work-iq-data-layer]], [[work-iq-memory-layer]] and [[work-iq-inference-layer]], with access through [[work-iq-api]] and [[work-iq-mcp]]. Details are evolving; verify in current documentation.

terms.summary: Work IQ is Microsoft's way of giving Copilot and agents an understanding of how your work happens.

levels.beginner: The Work IQ API lets approved apps and agents use Work IQ.
levels.maker: Developers use it to access contextual intelligence and related tools.
levels.architect: Subject to authentication and permissions; check the current capabilities.

terms.summary: The Work IQ API lets approved apps and agents use Work IQ.

levels.beginner: The data layer is the part of Work IQ that gathers signals from files, email, meetings and chats.
levels.maker: It builds a picture of how work happens.
levels.architect: Honours existing access controls; see [[work-iq]].

terms.summary: The data layer is the part of Work IQ that gathers signals from files, email, meetings and chats.

levels.beginner: The inference layer is where models, skills and tools work together on Work IQ context.
levels.maker: Agents use it to reason and take permitted actions.
levels.architect: See [[work-iq]] and [[inference]].

terms.summary: The inference layer is where models, skills and tools work together on Work IQ context.

levels.beginner: Work IQ MCP is a way for agents to use Work IQ through the standard MCP plug.
levels.maker: Supported agents can retrieve and act on Microsoft 365 work information through governed interfaces. Some capabilities may be in preview.
levels.architect: Uses [[model-context-protocol]]. Check preview status before relying on it.

terms.summary: Work IQ MCP is a way for agents to use Work IQ through the standard MCP plug.

levels.beginner: The memory layer builds lasting knowledge of work patterns and priorities.
levels.maker: Supported agents use it to keep context over time.
levels.architect: See [[memory]] and review privacy implications.

terms.summary: The memory layer builds lasting knowledge of work patterns and priorities.

levels.beginner: A work item process is the program that actually carries out a piece of queued work.
levels.maker: It is a process that runs a work item.
levels.architect: The process runs a work item. Work item types are identified with a [[work-item-type-identifier]].

terms.summary: A work item process is the program that actually carries out a piece of queued work.

levels.beginner: It is the unique code for a kind of work item.
levels.maker: It is a GUID that is used to identify a work item type.
levels.architect: The GUID names the type, which the [[work-item-process]] handles.

terms.summary: It is the unique code for a kind of work item.

levels.beginner: A workflow is a defined series of steps that moves work from start to finish.
levels.maker: It can combine people, apps, agents and automation.
levels.architect: Define triggers, steps, error handling and ownership. See [[power-automate]].

terms.summary: A workflow is a defined series of steps that moves work from start to finish.

levels.beginner: A workflow agent carries out or coordinates the steps of a process, instead of only chatting.
levels.maker: It is suited to repeatable processes with defined steps.
levels.architect: Combine with [[human-in-the-loop]] approvals for risky steps.

terms.summary: A workflow agent carries out or coordinates the steps of a process, instead of only chatting.

levels.beginner: A workflow association attaches a workflow to a list or a type of item so that it can run.
levels.maker: It is an association of a workflow template to a specific list or [[content-type]]. The [[declarative-workflow-association]] is the code-free kind.
levels.architect: It ties the template to the list or content type, so that workflows can start there.

terms.summary: A workflow association attaches a workflow to a list or a type of item so that it can run.

levels.beginner: The workflow configuration file is the settings sheet that pulls a workflow's parts together.
levels.maker: It is an implementation-specific file that is part of a workflow. It holds the information needed to create a workflow template from the specified markup and rules files and to associate it with a list.
levels.architect: It combines the [[workflow-markup-file]] and the rules into a template and ties it to a list.

terms.summary: The workflow configuration file is the settings sheet that pulls a workflow's parts together.

levels.beginner: A workflow history item is one entry in the story of what a workflow has done.
levels.maker: It is a list item that stores information about the current status of, and past actions for, a document or item associated with a workflow. It is stored in the [[workflow-history-list]].
levels.architect: Each item belongs to the [[workflow-history-list]].

terms.summary: A workflow history item is one entry in the story of what a workflow has done.

levels.beginner: The workflow history list is the logbook of a business process.
levels.maker: It is a list that stores the history of actions or tasks for a business process. It is made up of [[workflow-history-item|history items]].
levels.architect: It differs from the [[workflow-task-list]], which stores the sequence of tasks.

terms.summary: The workflow history list is the logbook of a business process.

levels.beginner: A workflow identifier is the unique code of a workflow.
levels.maker: It is a GUID that is used to identify a workflow.
levels.architect: The GUID names the workflow and is not the same as a [[workflow-association]].

terms.summary: A workflow identifier is the unique code of a workflow.

levels.beginner: The workflow markup file is the written description of what a workflow does.
levels.maker: It is a file that contains markup to specify the functional behaviour of a workflow.
levels.architect: The markup states the behaviour. The [[workflow-configuration-file]] uses it to build the template.

terms.summary: The workflow markup file is the written description of what a workflow does.

levels.beginner: A workflow task is one job in the chain of a business process.
levels.maker: It is an action or task in a sequence that is related to a built-in or user-defined business process. Tasks are kept in the [[workflow-task-list]].
levels.architect: The task is part of the sequence and is stored in the [[workflow-task-list]].

terms.summary: A workflow task is one job in the chain of a business process.

levels.beginner: The workflow task list is the to-do list of a business process.
levels.maker: It is a list that stores the sequence of actions or tasks for a business process. It differs from the [[workflow-history-list]].
levels.architect: The list holds [[workflow-task|workflow tasks]] in sequence.

terms.summary: The workflow task list is the to-do list of a business process.

levels.beginner: Workplace intelligence is understanding drawn from your organisation's data, relationships and activity.
levels.maker: It makes AI help more relevant to work.
levels.architect: See [[organisational-context]] and [[work-iq]].

terms.summary: Workplace intelligence is understanding drawn from your organisation's data, relationships and activity.

levels.beginner: A workspace is a lasting area that groups the content, tools and activity for one piece of work.
levels.maker: It supports projects and long-running agent tasks.
levels.architect: Check who can access it and how content is retained.

terms.summary: A workspace is a lasting area that groups the content, tools and activity for one piece of work.

levels.beginner: An XLSX file is a standard Excel spreadsheet file.
levels.maker: Copilot can read these as a source or create them as output.
levels.architect: The format is a zipped bundle of XML parts.

terms.summary: An XLSX file is a standard Excel spreadsheet file.

levels.beginner: XML is a text format that stores information inside labelled tags.
levels.maker: Many Office file formats and older systems use it.
levels.architect: Compare with [[json]], which is more common in modern APIs.

terms.summary: XML is a text format that stores information inside labelled tags.

levels.beginner: YAML is a readable text format often used for settings.
levels.maker: Developers use it for configuration and automation definitions.
levels.architect: It is whitespace-sensitive, so indentation errors are common. Compare with [[json]].

terms.summary: YAML is a readable text format often used for settings.

levels.beginner: Zero Trust means never assuming anyone is safe just because they are on the company network.
levels.maker: Every request is checked, rights are kept small and you plan as if a breach has happened.
levels.architect: Built on explicit verification, [[least-privilege]] and assume-breach. It applies equally to agents.

terms.summary: Zero Trust means never assuming anyone is safe just because they are on the company network.

levels.beginner: A zero-based index starts counting at 0, not 1, the way a ruler starts at zero.
levels.maker: It is an index in which the first item has an index of zero. Mind this when mixing it with one-based counts.
levels.architect: The first item is at 0. Off-by-one errors are common when a one-based number is passed to a zero-based API.

terms.summary: A zero-based index starts counting at 0, not 1, the way a ruler starts at zero.

levels.beginner: Zero-shot classification sorts items into categories without having been shown examples of those categories.
levels.maker: You just name the categories.
levels.architect: Accuracy varies; validate on samples. See [[zero-shot-learning]].

terms.summary: Zero-shot classification sorts items into categories without having been shown examples of those categories.

levels.beginner: Zero-shot learning is when a model handles a task it was not specifically trained on.
levels.maker: It relies on what the model learned in general.
levels.architect: Compare with [[zero-shot-prompting]].

terms.summary: Zero-shot learning is when a model handles a task it was not specifically trained on.

levels.beginner: Zero-shot prompting is asking the AI to do something with instructions only, without showing examples.
levels.maker: It is the simplest way to ask; add examples if results are poor.
levels.architect: See [[prompt-engineering]].

terms.summary: Zero-shot prompting is asking the AI to do something with instructions only, without showing examples.
